target: Ik kom uit Nederland.
english: I come from the Netherlands.
tip: 'Komen' (to come): 'ik kom' uses just the stem – Dutch drops -t for first person.

target: Hallo, mag ik binnenkomen?
english: Hello, may I come in?
tip: Modal verb sits second; the main verb jumps to the end. Ik moet morgen vroeg opstaan (I have to get up early tomorrow). Brackets the sentence.

target: Hoi, ik ben er weer!
english: Hi, I'm back!
tip: 'Ik ben' (I am) uses 'zijn' – the most irregular Dutch verb.

target: Goedemorgen, ik heb goed geslapen.
english: Good morning, I slept well.
tip: 'Hebben' (to have) drops its -t ending with 'ik': 'ik heb', not 'ik hebt'.

target: Ik zal je morgen bellen.
english: I will call you tomorrow.
tip: Modal verb sits second; the main verb jumps to the end. Ik moet morgen vroeg opstaan (I have to get up early tomorrow). Brackets the sentence.

target: Goedenavond, het eten is klaar.
english: Good evening, dinner is ready.
tip: 'Zijn' (to be) is fully irregular: 'ik ben', 'jij bent', 'hij is', 'wij zijn'.

target: Ik drink elke morgen koffie.
english: I drink coffee every morning.
tip: Dutch verb stems: remove -en, apply spelling rules (double vowels in closed syllables, devoice z→s, v→f).

target: Wij lopen door het bos.
english: We walk through the forest.
tip: 'Lopen' (to walk): 'ik loop', 'jij loopt' – vowel doubles in the stem.

target: Hallo, mijn naam is Jan.
english: Hello, my name is Jan.
tip: 'Is' comes from 'zijn' – used for identity, location, and as a perfect tense auxiliary.

target: Leuk je weer te spreken.
english: Nice to speak to you again.
tip: Dutch present tense: remove -en from the infinitive for the stem, then add endings.

target: Dag, ik moet nu gaan.
english: Bye, I have to go now.
tip: In Dutch, 'ik' always takes the bare verb stem – no -t or -en ending.

target: Hallo, ik zoek het station.
english: Hello, I am looking for the station.
tip: 'Zoeken' (to search): stem is 'zoek' – with 'ik', just use the stem.

target: Hallo, ik kom je ophalen.
english: Hello, I'm coming to pick you up.
tip: Dutch has two 'you's: `je/jij` (informal – friends, family, peers) and `u` (formal – strangers, elders, business). They use different verb forms: `jij hebt` vs `u hebt` (or `u heeft`).

target: Hij gaat zijn ouders bezoeken.
english: He is going to visit his parents.
tip: "Er" has multiple uses: existential, locative, and prepositional.

target: Prettig kennis met u te maken.
english: Pleased to make your acquaintance.
tip: `Je` (unstressed) vs `jij` (stressed/contrastive) – same word, just emphasis. Possessive: `je/jouw boek` (your book, informal) vs `uw boek` (formal).

target: Doei, ik zie je morgen weer!
english: Bye, I'll see you again tomorrow!
tip: Modern Dutch trends toward `je` even with strangers. But in customer service, with older people, or in writing – default to `u`.

target: Ik wens je een fijne dag.
english: I wish you a nice day.
tip: Plural is always `jullie` (you guys) – no formal plural. Even when addressing a group formally, `jullie` works. For very formal writing only, `u` covers both singular and plural.

target: Ik bel mijn moeder elke zondag.
english: I call my mother every Sunday.
tip: 'Mijn' (my) is a possessive pronoun – it doesn't change for de/het words.

target: Ik geloof dat hij gelijk heeft.
english: I believe that he is right.
tip: Subordinating conjunctions (`dat`, `omdat`, `als`, `terwijl`, `nadat`) send the verb to the end of the clause: `Ik weet dat hij komt`.

target: Hij rent elke ochtend vijf kilometer.
english: He runs five kilometers every morning.
tip: Third person (hij/ze) adds -t to the verb stem: 'hij werkt', 'ze woont'.

target: Ik reis vaak voor mijn werk.
english: I travel often for my work.
tip: In Dutch, 'ik' takes the verb stem: 'ik werk', while 'jij werkt' adds -t.

target: Ik bel mijn ouders elke week.
english: I call my parents every week.
tip: Possessives: mijn (my), jouw / je (your), zijn (his), haar (her), onze / ons (our), jullie (your pl), hun (their).

target: Wij brengen de kinderen naar school.
english: We bring the children to school.
tip: Plural subjects (wij/zij/ze) always take the infinitive form: 'wij werken', 'zij lopen'.

target: Wij eten samen in de keuken.
english: We eat together in the kitchen.
tip: 'Eten' (to eat): 'ik eet' – one-syllable stem needs double vowel for the long sound.

target: Zij leert elke dag nieuwe woorden.
english: She learns new words every day.
tip: When "jij" follows the verb in questions, the -t drops: "werk jij?" not "werkt jij?"

target: Zij heeft geen broers of zussen.
english: She has no brothers or sisters.
tip: `geen` negates a noun without article: `ik heb geen geld` (I have no money). `Niet` negates everything else: `ik kom niet` (I'm not coming).

target: Ik werk elke dag op kantoor.
english: I work every day at the office.
tip: Stem-final -z becomes -s: lezen -> ik lees, hij leest.

target: Het is tien over half vier nu.
english: It's ten minutes past three-thirty now.
tip: 'Tien over half vier' = 3:40 – ten past the half-hour mark before four.

target: Ik ben zo blij je te zien!
english: I am so happy to see you!
tip: Dutch has two 'you's: `je/jij` (informal – friends, family, peers) and `u` (formal – strangers, elders, business). They use different verb forms: `jij hebt` vs `u hebt` (or `u heeft`).

target: Mijn schoonmoeder komt vanavond eten.
english: My mother-in-law is coming for dinner tonight.
tip: "Schoonmoeder" – 'schoon' in family terms means 'in-law'.

target: Hij kookt vanavond pasta voor ons.
english: He cooks pasta for us tonight.
tip: 'Koken' (to cook): 'ik kook' – vowel doubles in the closed stem syllable.

target: De bus stopt bij elk station.
english: The bus stops at every station.
tip: Plural is always de: het kind (the child) → de kinderen (the children). Singular is where you need to remember the gender.

target: De kat slaapt op de bank.
english: The cat sleeps on the couch.
tip: Stem-final -v becomes -f in conjugation: leven -> ik leef, hij leeft.

target: Gisteren kocht zij een nieuwe fiets.
english: Yesterday she bought a new bicycle.
tip: Dutch follows V2 like German: the verb stays in second position. `Vandaag ga ik` (today I go), not `vandaag ik ga`. Subject jumps after the verb when something else opens the sentence.

target: De kinderen hebben geen honger meer.
english: The children are no longer hungry.
tip: `geen` negates a noun without article: `ik heb geen geld` (I have no money). `Niet` negates everything else: `ik kom niet` (I'm not coming).

target: Ik wil graag mijn excuses aanbieden.
english: I would like to offer my apologies.
tip: 'Willen' (to want) is irregular: 'ik wil', 'jij wilt', 'hij wil'.

target: Wij wonen dicht bij het centrum.
english: We live close to the city center.
tip: 'Wonen' (to live): stem is 'woon' – the vowel doubles to stay long in a closed syllable.

target: Ik ben net verhuisd naar Den Haag.
english: I just moved to The Hague.
tip: "Den Haag" is the Dutch name for The Hague – officially 's-Gravenhage.

target: Dag schat, ik heb je gemist vandaag.
english: Hi darling, I missed you today.
tip: Perfect = `hebben/zijn` + past participle. Most verbs use `hebben`: `ik heb gegeten`, `wij hebben gezien`. Participle to the end of the sentence.

target: Tot straks, ik ga even boodschappen doen.
english: See you later, I'm going grocery shopping.
tip: 'Gaan' (to go) is irregular: 'ik ga', 'jij gaat'. Used to express near future.

target: Hij bestelt een broodje haring met uitjes.
english: He orders a herring sandwich with onions.
tip: "Broodje haring" – raw herring with onions, a Dutch delicacy.

target: De kat slaapt altijd op de bank.
english: The cat always sleeps on the couch.
tip: Present tense: 'slapen' → 'slaapt' – long vowel 'aa' shortens to 'a' in open syllable.

target: De zon schijnt helder aan de hemel.
english: The sun shines brightly in the sky.
tip: Dutch present tense: stem + t for "jij/hij/zij": "hij werkt" (he works).

target: Zij leest graag boeken in de tuin.
english: She likes reading books in the garden.
tip: 'Lezen' (to read): stem is 'lees' – z devoices to s, vowel doubles to stay long.

target: Hij fietst elke ochtend naar zijn werk.
english: He cycles every morning to his work.
tip: Regular -en verbs: 'werken' → stem 'werk' + endings. 'Wij werken' keeps the infinitive form.

target: De stad is bekend om haar grachten.
english: The city is known for its canals.
tip: 'Zijn' + 'bekend om' = to be known for – describes a characteristic.

target: Ik woon al drie jaar in Rotterdam.
english: I have lived in Rotterdam for three years.
tip: With 'ik', the verb loses its -t ending: 'ik woon' (I live), but 'hij woont'.

target: Ik reis graag en ontmoet nieuwe mensen.
english: I like to travel and meet new people.
tip: 'Reizen' (to travel): 'ik reis' – the z becomes s in the stem due to Dutch spelling rules.

target: De supermarkt sluit om half tien vanavond.
english: The supermarket closes at half past nine tonight.
tip: Dutch 'half tien' = half TO ten = 9:30, not 10:30!

target: Mijn neef en nicht komen morgen op bezoek.
english: My nephew and niece are visiting tomorrow.
tip: 'Komen' is semi-regular: 'ik kom', 'jij komt', 'wij komen' – stem stays short.

target: Hallo, ik ben blij je weer te zien.
english: Hello, I am happy to see you again.
tip: `Je` (unstressed) vs `jij` (stressed/contrastive) – same word, just emphasis. Possessive: `je/jouw boek` (your book, informal) vs `uw boek` (formal).

target: Hij eet een uitsmijter met drie gebakken eieren.
english: He eats an uitsmijter with three fried eggs.
tip: "Uitsmijter" – open sandwich with fried eggs, ham, and cheese.

target: Hij eet drie boterhammen met pindakaas als lunch.
english: He eats three sandwiches with peanut butter for lunch.
tip: Adjectives before "het" nouns without "het" get no -e: "een groot huis" (a big house).

target: Hij neemt de waterbus over de Nieuwe Maas.
english: He takes the water bus across the Nieuwe Maas.
tip: 'Waterbus' = water bus/taxi – rotterdam public transport on water.

target: Ons gezin woont in een rijtjeshuis in Eindhoven.
english: Our family lives in a terraced house in Eindhoven.
tip: "Rijtjeshuis" – a row house, very typical Dutch housing.

target: Zij eet elke ochtend een boterham met hagelslag.
english: She eats a sandwich with chocolate sprinkles every morning.
tip: "Hagelslag" – chocolate sprinkles on bread, a Dutch breakfast staple.

target: Ik ben verkouden en moet in bed blijven.
english: I have a cold and must stay in bed.
tip: 'Zijn' for illness: 'verkouden zijn' = to have a cold – Dutch uses 'be' here.

target: Tot straks, ik ben over een uurtje terug.
english: See you later, I'll be back in about an hour.
tip: "Tot straks" means 'see you shortly' – implies a brief departure.

target: De fooi is vijftien procent van de totale rekening.
english: The tip is fifteen percent of the total bill.
tip: Tipping in the Netherlands: 5-15% is customary but not obligatory.

target: Ik stap over op een andere lijn bij station Sloterdijk.
english: I transfer to another line at station Sloterdijk.
tip: 'Overstappen' = to transfer – essential Dutch transit verb.
